children.author: apsurd
children.text: This is a very helpful explanation, thank you. The part about basically duck-typing an Agent's environment and tool access is particularly insightful.

There is a notion right now of decoupling the agent loop from the sandbox, so the sandbox isn't waiting for request-response from the agent. This would probably be 90+% of all the agent work.

If you combine this with products like Sprites from Fly.io (or OSS version - agent substrate), where you pay only per execution request in a sandbox, you can have huge savings compare to the event loop inside the sanbdox. You will be billed only for request executions (tens of milliseconds per read/write, hundreds of milliseconds per search, etc.) and zero for all the waiting time during the the inference phase.

Also, if you don't require a real Linux sandbox — you might actually emulate the environment, e.g. just-bash idea with linux-like environment to give agents something that looks like their native habitat, but under the hood, it can be just CF Durable Objects SQLite or whatever else.

Probably(?) almost all knowledge work doesn't require a Linux sandbox. You can just build a document reading and editing agent that does tool calls and connects to other products via MCPs, APIs, etc. And lightweight actors make a lot of sense to me in these cases.

children.author: NathanFlurry
children.text:
Hey!

> Wouldn't an agent in any capacity need a sandbox runtime to do agentic work?

Developers on Rivet use 3 different patterns:

- Just agents: many agents just need tools, such as customer support or personal agents

- Agents with lightweight sandbox: Rivet provides a V8 / WebAssembly sandboxing library for running JS & Python with a filesystem, which covers most workloads like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode (https://rivet.dev/agentos/)

- Agent outside of the sandbox: expose the sandbox to the agent as tools, which is better for blast radius, trust boundary, and orchestration (see below)

> Is the idea that state/memory/context and runtime env are separate concepts in rivet?

Exactly, Rivet Actors support running the harness outside of the sandbox. It's often referred to "separation of head from the hands."

I wrote a bit about why a while back: https://rivet.dev/blog/2026-07-27-run-your-harness-outside-t...

> When you say "sandboxes are too slow" do you mean needing to boot the sandbox to get back Agent state?

Specifically coldstarts. As LLMs are getting faster and have more realtime use cases, sandboxes are become the bottleneck on time to interactive for an agent.

Wouldn't an agent in any capacity need a sandbox runtime to do agentic work? When you say "sandboxes are too slow" do you mean needing to boot the sandbox to get back Agent state? Is the idea that state/memory/context and runtime env are separate concepts in rivet?

(I'm a professional developer but don't do any orchestration so trying to understand from basic mental model pov)

Been a minute since the gaming days, thanks for reaching out!

> Have you had agents like claude code , codex etc all fully running in agent-os?

We have gotten them all working inside of agentOS. However, we found it's a better architecture to run the agent loop outside of agentOS and expose it as tools. The trust boundary & blast radius of running the agent inside the sandbox makes it difficult.

Also, the memory overhead of running individual Claude Code instances is nuts, it's better to run the agents in a single process using tools.

I wrote a bit more on it here: https://rivet.dev/blog/2026-07-27-run-your-harness-outside-t...

> Also with the s3 backing changes, it reminds me a lot of the work done on celld, good to see more self-hostable durable objects out there.

Appreciate it!

Rivet has a much different architecture than most S3-backed databases. Having an object-per-actor doesn't scale well with cost and performance, so we built a SSD tiered storage engine instead: https://rivet.dev/changelog/2026-10-26-introducing-rivet-3-0...

Ping me on Discord if you give it a try, would be fun to catch up: https://rivet.dev/discord

children.author: takeitwhen
children.text: One thing that bit me running long agent workflows: hibernate/resume is great until tool results aren't part of the durable snapshot. If the actor wakes from SQLite alone and the previous turn's tool payload lived only in memory (or a temp file), the next step invents a confident continuation. We ended up treating "resume" as unsafe unless the last tool I/O was written into the same durable store as the conversation before suspend. Density numbers matter less than whether wake always reconstitutes enough to refuse to continue when that evidence is missing.

source.text:
Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3.

Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle.

It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable.

Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c

When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users.

As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes).

For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects.

Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost:

When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.

This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99).

We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere

Rivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust. Out of the box, they support agents (Pi Durable), workflows, real-time, multiplayer, running AI-generated code, Durable Streams, and integrations with tools like Vercel’s Eve and Turso. See all of our available guides, or point your agent at them: https://rivet.dev/docs/#guides

Try it out now, by reading our quickstart guides (https://rivet.dev/docs/) or ask your agent: “Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then build a multiplayer chat agent and run it locally.”

We’d love to get feedback on your experience with Rivet! We’re deeply invested in making Rivet an easy-to-self-host, flexible, and efficient way to run agentic workloads.

GitHub: https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet

Architecture: https://rivet.dev/docs/architecture/

Benchmarks: https://rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking/

Self-hosting: https://rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/

comments.author: NathanFlurry
comments.text: Been a minute since the gaming days, thanks for reaching out! > Have you had agents like claude code , codex etc all fully running in agent-os? We have gotten them all working inside of agentOS. However, we found it's a better architecture to run the agent loop outside of agentOS and expose it as tools. The trust boundary & blast radius of running the agent inside the sandbox makes it difficult. Also, the memory overhead of running individual Claude Code instances is nuts, it's better to run the agents in a single process using tools. I wrote a bit more on it here:  https://rivet.dev/blog/2026-07-27-run-your-harness-outside-t...  > Also with the s3 backing changes, it reminds me a lot of the work done on celld, good to see more self-hostable durable objects out there. Appreciate it! Rivet has a much different architecture than most S3-backed databases. Having an object-per-actor doesn't scale well with cost and performance, so we built a SSD tiered storage engine instead:  https://rivet.dev/changelog/2026-10-26-introducing-rivet-3-0...  Ping me on Discord if you give it a try, would be fun to catch up:  https://rivet.dev/discord

comments.author: Tanjreeve
comments.text: In OP > It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost: > When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.

comments.author: NathanFlurry
comments.text: Hey! Rivet includes a library for running untrusted user code called agentOS:  https://rivet.dev/agentos/  It provides Linux-compatible sandboxing using V8 / WebAssembly. Supports full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. Security-wise, it's the same model as Cloudflare Workers & Chromium. Rivet is frequently used for running the harness outside of the sandbox. Wrote a bit about why here:  https://rivet.dev/blog/2026-07-27-run-your-harness-outside-t...

comments.author: looplilt
comments.text: Keeping S3 off the write path is the design choice that makes the whole pitch click for me: acknowledging a write once two of three availability zones have it on SSD, then batching to object storage in the background, gets durability without paying object-storage latency on every turn. That also explains why separating the agent loop from the sandbox matters, since a long-running turn shouldn't have to keep a heavyweight environment warm just to hold its state. My main question is how that tiering behaves when an actor wakes after a long idle period and its data has fully cooled to S3: is that 138 ms read the typical cost, or does it get worse with larger session transcripts and filesystems?

comments.author: sebastienburel

Messages are queued and only handled once the current handler returns, so a synchronous handler is never cut in half. But while a handler waits on an async call, an HTTP request say, other messages still get handled. So “no message being processed” isn’t the same as “nothing in flight”. Does Rivet hibernate an actor with an outstanding request, and if so, what happens when the response comes back?

comments.author: takeitwhen
comments.text: One thing that bit me running long agent workflows: hibernate/resume is great until tool results aren't part of the durable snapshot. If the actor wakes from SQLite alone and the previous turn's tool payload lived only in memory (or a temp file), the next step invents a confident continuation. We ended up treating "resume" as unsafe unless the last tool I/O was written into the same durable store as the conversation before suspend. Density numbers matter less than whether wake always reconstitutes enough to refuse to continue when that evidence is missing.
